::: {.lead}
On a rocky island stands a lighthouse. At night its lamp turns around the
upright y-axis, and the beam must find each ship on the sea. A tank in
another game drives across a 3D map; its turret turns on top, and the
barrel turns with the turret. In lecture 13 you put the move, the scale and
the turn of a 2D object into one 3 × 3 matrix. A 3D game does the same with
one more coordinate: the point (x, y, z) becomes (x, y, z, 1), and every
transformation is a 4 × 4 matrix. In this lesson you move and scale in 3D,
you turn around the y-axis (yaw), meet the turns around x and z (pitch and
roll), and follow a point through a hierarchy of parent and child objects.
Every section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary 3d homogeneous-coordinates translation-matrix scaling rotation-axis rotation-matrix trs-matrix transform-hierarchy local-space forward-vector >}}

## 14.1 From 3 × 3 to 4 × 4: translation in 3D

In 3D, a point has three coordinates. As in lecture 13, we add w = 1: the
point (x, y, z) becomes (x, y, z, 1), and a transformation is a 4 × 4 matrix
(@fig-t4).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 14.1 — Translation in 3D"}
The **translation matrix** that moves every point by (tx, ty, tz) is
$$T(t_x, t_y, t_z) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & t_x \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & t_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & t_z \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}.$$
The move is in the last column; the last row is (0, 0, 0, 1). Directions
have w = 0 and are not moved.
:::

![T(3, 0, 4) moves the crate at (1, 0, 2) to (4, 0, 6).](images/translate-4x4.png){#fig-t4 width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 14.1 — Moving a crate"}
A crate stands at (1, 0, 2). It slides by (3, 0, 4).

1. Row 1: 1 + 0 + 0 + 3 × 1 = **4**.
2. Row 2: 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = **0**. Row 3: 2 + 4 = **6**.
3. The crate is at (4, 0, 6). T(−3, 0, −4) brings it back.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Forgetting the fourth coordinate. A 4 × 4 matrix cannot multiply (x, y, z):
write (x, y, z, 1) for a point and (x, y, z, 0) for a direction.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Build T(1, 2, 3)"}
1. Write T(1, 2, 3).
2. Multiply it by the point (4, 0, 0, 1) and by the direction (4, 0, 0, 0).

*Your result:* one matrix and two results.
:::

## 14.2 Scaling in 3D

A pillar in a temple is a cube made 4 units tall. A 3D scaling has one
factor for each axis (@fig-s3).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 14.2 — Scaling in 3D"}
$$S(s_x, s_y, s_z) = \begin{bmatrix} s_x & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & s_y & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & s_z & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}.$$
It multiplies x by sx, y by sy and z by sz, around the origin (the pivot of
the object). With sx = sy = sz it is a uniform scaling.
:::

![S(2, 3, 1) makes the unit cube 2 wide, 3 tall and 1 deep.](images/scale-3d.png){#fig-s3 width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 14.2 — A tall box"}
The corner (1, 1, 1) of the unit cube with S(2, 3, 1):

1. x: 2 × 1 = 2. y: 3 × 1 = 3. z: 1 × 1 = 1.
2. The corner goes to **(2, 3, 1)**: the box is 2 wide, 3 tall, 1 deep.
3. In Unity this is the Scale (2, 3, 1) in the Inspector.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that "scale 2" doubles the volume. A uniform scale of 2 doubles
every side, so the volume grows 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 times.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · A pillar"}
1. Which scaling turns the unit cube into a pillar 1 wide, 4 tall and 1
   deep?
2. Where does the corner (1, 1, 1) go?

*Your result:* one matrix and one point.
:::

## 14.3 Yaw: turning around the y-axis

In 3D, a rotation turns around an **axis**. The lighthouse lamp and the tank
turn around the upright y-axis; this turn is the **yaw**. The y coordinate
stays the same; x and z mix like x and y did in 2D (@fig-yaw).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 14.3 — Rotation around the y-axis"}
$$R_y(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & 0 & \sin\theta \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\sin\theta & 0 & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}.$$
In 4 × 4 form, add the last row and column (0, 0, 0, 1). The forward vector (0, 0, 1) goes to **(sin θ, 0, cos θ)**. In Unity (y up,
z forward), a positive yaw turns to the right, seen from above.
:::

![Seen from above: R_y(θ) turns the forward vector (0, 0, 1) to (sin θ, 0, cos θ). At 90° it points to the right, along x.](images/yaw.png){#fig-yaw width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 14.3 — The beam at 90°"}
The lamp of the lighthouse looks forward, along (0, 0, 1). It turns by 90°:
cos 90° = 0, sin 90° = 1.

1. Row 1: 0 × 0 + 0 × 0 + 1 × 1 = **1**.
2. Row 2: 0. Row 3: −1 × 0 + 0 + 0 × 1 = **0**.
3. The beam points along (1, 0, 0): to the right. A ship at (10, 0, 0) is in
   the light.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 14.4 — A point to the right"}
The tank's right side is at (2, 0, 0). Turn by 90°:

1. Row 1: cos 90° × 2 = 0. Row 3: −sin 90° × 2 = **−2**.
2. The point goes to **(0, 0, −2)**: what was on the right is now behind.
3. Check with Yaw Lab: after a right turn, the right side points back.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/yaw-lab.html" poster="sims/yaw-lab.png" title="Yaw Lab: turning around the y-axis in 3D" height="820" >}}

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
```csharp
transform.rotation = Quaternion.Euler(0, 30, 0);   // a yaw of 30°
Vector3 f = transform.forward;                     // (0.5, 0, 0.87)
transform.Rotate(0, 90 * Time.deltaTime, 0);       // turn right at 90° per second
```
`transform.forward` is the rotation applied to (0, 0, 1).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Using the 2D matrix with sin θ in row 1 as −sin θ. Around the y-axis, the
minus sign is in **row 3**: R_y(90°) must send (0, 0, 1) to (1, 0, 0).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Yaw by hand, check in Yaw Lab"}
1. Compute R_y(180°) × (0, 0, 1) and R_y(−90°) × (0, 0, 1).
2. In **Yaw Lab**, set θ = 180° and θ = −90°, and compare with the forward
   vector shown.

*Your result:* two vectors from paper and the same two from the lab.
:::

## 14.4 Pitch and roll: the other two axes

An aircraft also lifts its nose (**pitch**, around x) and tips its wings
(**roll**, around z). Each turn keeps its own axis and mixes the other two
coordinates (@fig-axes).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 14.4 — Rotations around x and z"}
$$R_x(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ 0 & \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}, \qquad R_z(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}.$$
R_z is the 2D rotation of lecture 12 with z kept. Unity applies the three
turns of `Quaternion.Euler(x, y, z)` in the order z, then x, then y.
:::

![Pitch, yaw and roll. The axis of each turn keeps its 1.](images/three-axes.png){#fig-axes width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 14.5 — Nose down, wing up"}
1. Pitch 90°: R_x(90°) × (0, 0, 1) = (0, −1, 0). A positive pitch in Unity
   points the nose **down**.
2. Roll 90°: R_z(90°) × (1, 0, 0) = (0, 1, 0). The right wing points **up**.
3. Yaw 90°: R_y(90°) × (0, 0, 1) = (1, 0, 0), as in section 14.3.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Changing the order of the turns. As in 2D, R_x × R_y is not R_y × R_x: a
pitch then a yaw ends somewhere else than a yaw then a pitch.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Which axis?"}
1. A car drives up a ramp. Which turn is it: pitch, yaw or roll?
2. Compute R_z(180°) × (1, 2, 0).

*Your result:* one word and one vector.
:::

## 14.5 The TRS matrix in 3D and the hierarchy

Every object in a 3D scene has a position, a rotation and a scale: its
**TRS matrix** M = T × R × S, now 4 × 4. Objects are also put inside other
objects: the turret is a **child** of the tank (@fig-tree).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 14.5 — Transform hierarchy"}
In a **transform hierarchy**, a child's position, rotation and scale are in
its parent's local space. Its world matrix is
$$M_\text{world}(\text{child}) = M_\text{world}(\text{parent}) \times M_\text{local}(\text{child}).$$
When the parent moves or turns, all its children move and turn with it.
:::

![The barrel tip is a child of the turret, the turret a child of the tank.](images/hierarchy.png){#fig-tree width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 14.6 — The barrel tip in the world"}
The tank stands at (10, 0, 5) with a yaw of 90°. The turret is at (0, 1, 0)
on the tank; the barrel tip is at (0, 0, 2) on the turret.

1. In the tank's space: (0, 1, 0) + (0, 0, 2) = (0, 1, 2).
2. Yaw 90°: R_y(90°) × (0, 1, 2) = (2, 1, 0).
3. + the tank's position: **(12, 1, 5)**.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
```csharp
Matrix4x4 m = Matrix4x4.TRS(new Vector3(10, 0, 5),
                            Quaternion.Euler(0, 90, 0), Vector3.one);
Vector3 tip = m.MultiplyPoint3x4(new Vector3(0, 1, 2));    // (12, 1, 5)
turret.transform.SetParent(tank.transform);                 // the turret follows the tank
```
`transform.localPosition` is the position in the parent's space;
`transform.position` is the world position.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Adding the child's local position to the parent's position without the
turn. (10, 0, 5) + (0, 1, 2) = (10, 1, 7) is wrong when the tank is turned.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The tank turns back"}
The same tank stands at (10, 0, 5) with a yaw of 180°.

1. Where is the barrel tip (0, 1, 2), in the tank's space, in the world?
2. The tank drives to (0, 0, 0) with a yaw of 0. Where is the tip now?

*Your result:* two points.
:::

## Case study: Lighthouse

*Lighthouse* is a made-up night game. The lighthouse stands at the origin;
its lamp turns around the y-axis, and at the yaw θ the beam points along
R_y(θ) × (0, 0, 1) = (sin θ, 0, cos θ). Ships wait 10 units away: at
(10, 0, 0), at (0, 0, −10), at (5, 0, 8.7) and at (−7.1, 0, 7.1). The player
must choose the yaw for each ship, and then the turn from 90° to a ship at
(−10, 0, 0). The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses these
numbers. In the mini-game below you turn the lamp.

{{< sim file="sims/lighthouse.html" poster="sims/lighthouse.png" title="Lighthouse: light up the ships with a yaw" kind="game" height="820" >}}

## Further reading

Dunn and Parberry, *3D Math Primer for Graphics and Game Development*,
2nd ed., Chapter 5 (rotation, scaling and 4 × 4 matrices in 3D) and
Chapter 8 (Euler angles: heading, pitch and bank).

## Exercises

1. Write the point (2, 5, −1) in homogeneous coordinates.
2. Compute T(1, 2, 3) × (4, 0, 0, 1).
3. Which matrix undoes T(1, 2, 3)?
4. Apply S(2, 2, 2) to the point (1, −1, 3).
5. The unit cube gets S(1, 4, 1). How tall is it now?
6. Write R_y(90°) as a 3 × 3 matrix.
7. Compute R_y(90°) × (0, 0, 1).
8. Compute R_y(180°) × (3, 2, 1).
9. Compute R_y(90°) × (2, 0, 0).
10. A player has a yaw of 30° (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.87). What is the
    forward vector?
11. Around which axis is the pitch? And the roll?
12. Compute R_x(90°) × (0, 0, 1). Where does the nose point?
13. A tank stands at (0, 0, 0) with a yaw of 0. The barrel tip is at
    (0, 1, 2) in the tank's space. Where is it in the world?
14. The tank stands at (10, 0, 5) with a yaw of 180°. Where is the barrel
    tip (0, 1, 2) in the world?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. (2, 5, −1, 1).
2. (5, 2, 3, 1).
3. T(−1, −2, −3).
4. (2, −2, 6).
5. 4 units (a pillar).
6. Rows (0, 0, 1), (0, 1, 0), (−1, 0, 0).
7. (1, 0, 0).
8. cos 180° = −1, sin 180° = 0: (−3, 2, −1).
9. (0, 0, −2).
10. (sin 30°, 0, cos 30°) = (0.5, 0, 0.87).
11. Pitch: around x. Roll: around z.
12. (0, −1, 0): the nose points down.
13. (0, 1, 2).
14. R_y(180°) × (0, 1, 2) = (0, 1, −2); + (10, 0, 5) = (10, 1, 3).
:::
